Side by side, and how they were read
Pairs of letters, the people Paul greets, and how the church received them.
TWIN LETTERS
Ephesians and Colossians
Thirty-one passages that run in parallel. Click a ribbon to keep it.

Thirty-one passages that run in parallel, paired from reading both letters and checked against Easton's list. Each weight is the number of distinct content words (by Strong's number, leaving out the commonest words) the two passages share in the Textus Receptus, so it measures shared vocabulary, not shared ideas. Other measures differ: ISBE finds 78 of Ephesians' 155 verses in Colossians "in varying degrees of identity"; Easton, quoting an older writer, counts about forty-two parallels. The household code (wives, husbands, children, fathers, servants, masters) runs in the same order in both. Ephesians 5:22–6:9 Colossians 3:18–4:1 [8][14]
ROMANS 16
The people of Paul's greetings
Every name in Romans 16. Choose a person to see who they were and where else Scripture names them.

Phebe (Phoebe) A servant of the church at Cenchrea, commended to Rome; probably the bearer of the letter. our sister ... a succourer of many, and of myself also a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea receive her in the Lord ... assist her BRIDGE Romans 16:1–2 Romans 16:1 Romans 16:2
The church at Cenchrea a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea CHURCH Romans 16:1
The believers at Rome receive her in the Lord ... assist her CHURCH Romans 1:7 Romans 16:2 Romans 16:3–4 +11 more

Paul greets 24 believers at Rome by name, and two households, though he had never been there; eight people with him at Corinth send their own greetings; and Phebe of Cenchrea, carrying his commendation, links the two. Each line carries Paul's own words about the person. Easton counts the same twenty-four. Romans 16:1–23 [14]
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
8 questions about these letters. Each answer is shown with the people who held it; this page does not choose between them.
North Galatia

Earlier scholars up to Lightfoot and Salmon; later Chase, Dods, Sabatier, Harnack, H. Holtzmann, Jülicher, Lipsius, Mommsen, Schmiedel, Schürer and others; Findlay himself (as listed by Findlay, ISBE)

The letter went to churches in old Galatia around Ancyra, Pessinus and Tavium, which Paul first reached on his second journey when he passed through "the region of Galatia". On this view the letter is later rather than earlier. Robertson judged in 1915 that it "still has the weight of authority". Acts 16:6 Acts 18:23 [5][18][1]
South Galatia
First proposed by Mynster (1825); then Perrot, Renan, Pfleiderer, Weizsäcker, Ramsay, von Soden, Bartlet, Gifford, Rendall, Sanday ("with hesitation") and others (as listed by Findlay, ISBE)

The letter went to Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, the churches Paul founded on his first journey, all inside the Roman province of Galatia. Ramsay's books made this view widely known from 1895, and some of its supporters make Galatians the earliest of Paul's letters. Acts 13:14–14:23 [17][5][1]
